lines: MARA: I watch the bluff birds at sunrise. I brought a partner to swap.
The river is high today. I keep my partners back from the bank.
My NATU keeps staring toward the bluffs. I wonder what it sees.
Home is a good place to rest before taking the trail.
I count every partner before we leave. Someone always stops to smell flowers.
Race you to the next bend! After I tie my shoes.
A short walk with your partner beats sitting inside all day.
The whole neighborhood comes out when the river breeze picks up.
IRIS: My MAGNEMITE helps sort clinic tools. I would like a garden partner.
Even trainers need water and a break. Look after yourself, too.
My partner used to fear checkups. Now it leads me to the clinic.
Visitors from all over stop here. A friendly face helps a long day.
I made a recovery card with little leaf prints.
Different partners need different care. Watch how yours behaves.
I take a lap between visits. Fresh air clears my head.
I am delivering flowers. Slowly. They spill if I run.
OTTO: My MACHOP hauls supplies uphill. I want a friend for the river.
The hill looks gentler from the top. My knees disagree.
Mud on the boots means a good river walk.
I roll snowballs down this slope in winter. Not at people!
We sketch the valley from here. No two drawings look alike.
Take the long way once. You notice more on the return.
Uphill, breathe. Downhill, watch your footing.
My partner and I practice our turns on this flat stretch.
SUE: My DROWZEE naps through bird calls. Perhaps a new partner will wake me up.
The granite holds the warmth after the sun moves on.
I can hear the river before I see it.
Students always ask where the bridge goes. Across the river, of course.
I leave time for the garden on my way home.
Good knots matter on a lake, too.
One more lap before lessons!
My partner likes the southern bank best. Fewer footsteps.
LEN: My SLOWPOKE waits beside every fishing hole. I need a sturdy trail partner.
Pack out the line and hooks you bring to the lake.
My grandpa says he saw a giant fish. His hands get farther apart each year.
Cabin weekends begin with a stop for supplies.
The old camp stories get better every summer.
I listen for loons when the boats go quiet.
I am walking off my breakfast before we launch.
If the fish are not biting, enjoy the view.
JO: I raised this POLIWAG by the cabin. Could you bring me a WOOPER?
The cabin smells of pine even with the windows shut.
Check the wind before you launch. It changes out on the lake.
Give nesting birds room. The shore is their home first.
I am learning every bird call. My loon still sounds like a squeaky door.
Coffee on the porch is my favorite part of the trip.
I walk down here when the morning mist lifts.
A loose knot makes for a very short fishing story.
HAL: This PINECO followed my timber cart home. I would like an ODDISH for the garden.
The tall tales grow a little taller every time they are told.
I made a scarf for my partner. It prefers to carry it.
You can spend a whole day watching the light change on the lake.
Count tree rings on fallen wood. Leave living trees alone.
My snow fort had three rooms. Then spring arrived.
I like this boardwalk. There is always somebody to greet.
I brought lunch for the crew. They can smell it from here.
ED: My TEDDIURSA has a nose for picnic baskets. I am curious about cave partners.
The mill whistle used to set the rhythm of the town.
A good story can travel farther than a canoe.
We trade books when we finish them. Partners make good listeners.
Some days I only catch my own reflection.
I am saving a smooth stone from every place we visit.
I follow the river walk before heading east.
My partner stops at every patch of shade.
NELL: My CHINCHOU lights up the evening. I would like a partner from the shore grass.
The bakery gets busy before the boats leave.
I can never mix quite the right lake blue.
A calm harbor can hide rough water outside.
That long lake horizon always makes me stop.
We came for the shore and stayed for the neighbors.
I stretch my legs before taking the north trail.
I check the weather twice before a crossing.
KIT: This WOOPER likes the shallows. A MARILL would be fine canoe company.
Speak softly by the water. You hear much more.
Wet boots outside the tent. I learned that lesson once.
We spotted tracks at camp. We left them for the next visitor.
Carry less, notice more. That is my portage advice.
I put every scrap back in my pack, even the tiny ones.
A short walk gives paddling arms a rest.
Quiet water is worth protecting.
ADA: My HOPPIP drifts over the meadow. I would like a curious forest friend.
Such a long river begins in such a small place.
I drew the headwaters on a postcard for my sister.
I keep the bank clean so the next person sees it this way.
We brought lunch and plenty of time.
I tried to follow one leaf downstream. It was faster than me.
The pine shade makes this a fine walking stop.
A spring needs care all along its banks.
BEA: My SKARMORY has crossed many ridges. I would like a stone trail partner.
Rest before a big challenge. There is no prize for arriving tired.
Everyone remembers their first trip north.
Canoes in summer, snowshoes in winter. There is always a way out.
I am writing down the constellations I saw at camp.
Win or lose, there will be a hot meal waiting.
I take one quiet lap before I register.
Someday I will challenge the League. Today I am practicing.
TESS: My MACHOP helped at the mill. I would like an ABRA for quiet study.
You can feel the falls through the rail when the river is high.
We rehearse in the music room. You can hear us down the block.
The old mills fed more than this city.
Keep a hand on your hat near the river.
I am choosing a book for my partner. It likes the pictures.
I warm up on the neighborhood streets before a battle.
The co-op knows everybody by their shopping basket.
The current carries energy. Watching it never gets old.
A river city always has one more bridge to cross.
A stage needs listeners as much as performers.
My partner keeps time with its feet.
Take a seat after your errands. The city will wait.
I deliver papers, then practice my throws.
I like a route with a good view between battles.
Neighbors keep the streets warm even when the weather does not.
REMY: My GROWLITHE loves a parade. I am looking for a sleepy reading companion.
The archives keep ordinary letters, too. Every life leaves a story.
I am saving room for one more fair snack.
These hills make every grocery trip a little workout.
Our class is drawing the capitol today.
The river is a different color after rain.
I walk past the old houses before practice.
The market smells different at every corner.
I still remember my first ride into this station.
Ask about the building, and someone will tell you a story.
My partner likes the noisy fair. I like the quiet walk home.
Freight comes and goes. The river keeps moving.
I am counting steps uphill. I lose count downhill.
A little garden brings plenty of tiny visitors.
My partner and I never skip our evening lap.
Come back with an appetite when the fair opens.
GUS: My SEEL loves the cold lake. I need a strong partner to help with ropes.
If the lake disappears in fog, listen for the horn.
The hill streets have given me very strong legs.
We watch for ships from the lookout.
Iron ore starts far inland. The harbor is only one part of the trip.
A warm kitchen feels better after lake wind.
Stairs are part of my daily training.
Check the line before putting your weight on it.
I wave at every ship. Sometimes someone waves back.
The lake changes the weather on both sides of town.
A working harbor has room for wildlife if we take care.
I packed a jacket. It is always the right choice here.
I draw boats while my partner watches gulls.
The best stories arrive with the crews.
One lap by the lake, then back up the hill.
No catch is worth leaving a hook on the shore.
